mainTopic: Wind-carried damage as 'his arrows', then the משנה on how far trees must be from a neighbor's field, with stories about palm trees, vines and roots.
overview: The amud opens with the last words of an earlier discussion: shaking counts as damage when it is strong enough to rattle a jug's lid. Next comes the case of flax chaff that flew off and hurt people. רבינא ruled the flax-beaters were not liable because the wind carried the chaff. מר בר רב אשי and מרימר disagreed, comparing it to winnowing on שבת, where wind help still counts as the person's own act. The גמרא explains why, for רבינא, a hammer's spark is different: the smith wants the spark to fly away. A new משנה then teaches that a tree must be planted four אמות from a neighbor's field, and that the neighbor may cut roots that spread into his land. שמואל says that in בבל two אמות are enough, and a ברייתא backs him up. Two stories follow. In the first, רב יוסף demands that palm trees near his vines be cut down. In the second, רב הונא cuts the roots of רב פפא's palms while digging pits, and רב פפא admits he could not convince him. That story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: How much shaking counts: enough to rattle a jug's lid
steps.stepSummary: The tail end of an earlier discussion: shaking counts as damage when it is strong enough to make the lid on a jug move.
steps.simpleTranslation: It counts when the lid on the mouth of a jug shakes.
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes an earlier discussion that started before this section. It gives the measure of how strong the shaking must be: strong enough to make a jug's lid move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question this answers ('how much?') came before this section begins. The answer gives a simple test anyone can see: if the lid on a jug moves, the shaking is strong enough to matter.

phrases.english: Enough that the lid shakes
on the mouth of a jug.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּדְנָיֵיד נִכְתְּמָא אַפּוּמֵּיהּ דְּחַצְבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes a discussion that began before this section.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The shaking must be strong enough to make a jug's lid move.

steps.title: The case of the flying flax chaff
steps.stepSummary: Chaff from the flax that בר מריון's household beat flew off and hurt people, and those people came to רבינא.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the household of בר מריון, son of רבין, when they beat flax, the chaff would fly off and harm people. The people came before רבינא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real-life case and brings it to רבינא for a ruling. This step sets up the question; the answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The important detail is that the chaff did not hit people directly from the beating. It floated off and travelled to them. That detail decides the ruling in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Chaff, tiny fibers that fly off flax

phrases.english: The household of בר מריון, son of רבין,
when they would beat flax,
the chaff would fly off
and harm people.
They came before רבינא.
phrases.notes: The ones who came are the people being hurt, coming to complain.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּבֵי בַּר מָרִיּוֹן בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבִין, כִּי הֲוָה נָפְצִי כִּיתָּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: a practical case about damage from flying chaff.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the flax-beater responsible for chaff that drifts and harms people?

steps.title: רבינא rules: the wind carried it, so it is not 'his arrows'
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says that רבי יוסי admits liability only when the damage moves by the person's own force. Here the wind carries the chaff, so the flax-beaters are not liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: When we say that רבי יוסי admits about 'his arrows', that is only when the thing travels by his own force. Here, it is the wind that carries it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא rules in favor of the flax-beaters. Their own force did not send the chaff; the wind did.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי usually says the person being harmed must protect himself. He admits that the damager must stop when the harm comes from 'his arrows', meaning things his own action sends out. רבינא limits that rule to things moved by the person's direct force. Wind-carried chaff falls outside it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'His arrows': harm sent out directly by a person's action

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the main question of the section: does help from the wind cancel the idea of 'his arrows'?

phrases.english: He said to them:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אָמְרִינַן מוֹדֶה רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּגִירֵי דִּילֵיהּ –
phrases.english: When we say that רבי יוסי admits regarding 'his arrows',
phrases.notes: 'His arrows' means harm a person sends out himself, like shooting an arrow at someone.

phrases.english: that is only when it travels by his own force.

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא – זִיקָא הוּא דְּקָא מַמְטֵי לַהּ.
phrases.english: Here, it is the wind that carries it.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אָמְרִינַן מוֹדֶה רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּגִירֵי דִּילֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the case brought in step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Not liable: 'his arrows' covers only direct force, and here the wind moved the chaff.

steps.title: מר בר רב אשי objects from winnowing on שבת
steps.stepSummary: מר בר רב אשי asks how this differs from winnowing on שבת, where the wind helps and it still counts as the person's own act.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בר רב אשי challenged this: How is this different from someone who winnows while the wind helps him?
steps.whatsHappening: מר בר רב אשי challenges רבינא's ruling with a case from the laws of שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a person winnows, he throws grain in the air and the wind blows the chaff away. That is a forbidden מלאכה on שבת even though the wind does part of the job. So wind help does not stop an act from being his own, and the same should be true for flax chaff.

keyTerms.meaning: One who winnows, a forbidden מלאכה on שבת

phrases.aramaic: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: מר בר רב אשי challenged this:
How is this different from one who winnows
phrases.notes: He is pointing to the laws of שבת, where winnowing is a forbidden מלאכה.

phrases.english: and the wind helps him?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי: מַאי שְׁנָא מִזּוֹרֶה וְרוּחַ מְסַיַּיעְתּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבינא's ruling in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's claim that wind-carried damage is not the person's own force.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: On שבת, winnowing with wind help counts as the person's own act. So wind help should not remove liability here either.

steps.title: מרימר agrees: it is just like winnowing with the wind
steps.stepSummary: The objection was brought to מרימר, who said the flax case is the same as winnowing with the wind's help.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said it before מרימר. He said to them: This is the same as one who winnows and the wind helps him.
steps.whatsHappening: מרימר sides with מר בר רב אשי's objection. He says the flax chaff counts as the person's own act, just like winnowing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wind help counts as the person's own force on שבת, so it also counts that way for damages. By this view, the flax-beaters would be responsible for the chaff.
steps.whatToRemember: According to מר בר רב אשי and מרימר, damage that the wind helps carry still counts as 'his arrows', just like winnowing on שבת.

phrases.english: They said it before מרימר,
he said to them:
This is the same as one who winnows and the wind helps him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמְרוּהָ קַמֵּיהּ דְּמָרִימָר, אֲמַר לְהוּ: הַיְינוּ זוֹרֶה וְרוּחַ מְסַיַּיעְתּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Agrees with the objection of step 4 against רבינא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: מרימר: beating flax with wind-carried chaff is like winnowing, so it counts as the person's own force.

steps.title: For רבינא: why is a hammer's spark different?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבינא would explain the case of a spark that flies from a hammer and causes damage, where the person must pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבינא, how is this different from a spark that comes out from under a hammer and causes damage, where he must pay?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבינא again, this time with a damages case: a spark from a hammer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A spark also flies off from the work and lands somewhere else before it causes damage, yet the smith must pay. That looks just like chaff flying off the beaten flax. The question pushes רבינא to explain what sets the two cases apart.

phrases.english: And according to רבינא,

phrases.aramaic: מַאי שְׁנָא מִגֵּץ הַיּוֹצֵא מִתַּחַת הַפַּטִּישׁ
phrases.english: how is this different from a spark that comes out from under the hammer
and causes damage, where he must pay?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרָבִינָא, מַאי שְׁנָא מִגֵּץ הַיּוֹצֵא מִתַּחַת הַפַּטִּישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to רבינא's view from step 3 and tests it against another case.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's ruling that the flax-beater is not liable.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A spark that flies off from a hammer and damages elsewhere makes the person liable. Chaff flying off beaten flax seems no different, so the flax-beater should be liable too.

steps.title: The smith wants the spark to fly away; the flax-beater does not care
steps.stepSummary: The smith wants the spark to fly away from him, but the flax-beater gains nothing from the chaff travelling.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, he wants it to go. Here, he does not care that it goes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבינא. The difference is whether the person wants the thing to fly away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The smith wants the spark to fly as far as possible from him, so its flight counts as part of his own act. The flax-beater gains nothing from the chaff travelling, so where it lands is the wind's doing, not his.

keyTerms.meaning: He is pleased with it, he wants it

steps.whatToRemember: For רבינא, something that flies off a person's work counts as 'his arrows' when he wants it to fly away, like a smith's spark. Flax chaff, which he does not care about and which the wind carries, is not his responsibility.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבינא is saying the spark doesn't travel. Both travel. The only difference is whether the person wants it to go.

phrases.english: There, he wants it to go,
phrases.notes: 'There' is the spark. The smith would rather it fly far from him.

phrases.english: here, he does not care that it goes.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם נִיחָא לֵיהּ דְּלֵיזִל, הָכָא לָא נִיחָא לֵיהּ דְּלֵיזִל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (חילוק): the spark case differs because the person wants the spark to fly away.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Anything that flies off a person's work and damages makes him liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: Liability for wind-carried damage applies only when the person wants it to travel. The flax-beater does not care, so רבינא's ruling stands.

steps.title: A tree must be four cubits from a neighbor's field
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a tree or grapevine must be planted four אמות away from a neighbor's field. If a fence stands between the fields, each owner may plant right up to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person may not plant a tree near his neighbor's field unless he keeps it four cubits away. This applies to grapevines and to every other tree. If there is a fence between the fields, each owner may plant right up against the fence on his own side.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a basic rule about how far trees must be kept from a neighbor's field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The planter has to keep a space of four אמות so that his tree does not harm the field next door. A fence changes the law because it already separates the two fields. With a fence in place, both owners may plant right next to it.

phrases.english: MISHNA
A person may not plant a tree
near his fellow's field
unless he distanced it from it
four cubits
whether grapevines or any tree
If there was a fence between them
this one may plant close to the fence on this side
phrases.notes: Literally "leans on the fence". It means he may plant right up against it.

phrases.english: and that one may plant close to the fence on that side

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא יִטַּע אָדָם אִילָן סָמוּךְ לִשְׂדֵה חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה with a new topic, separate from the flax and spark discussion
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A tree must be planted four אמות from a neighbor's field. With a fence between the fields, each owner may plant right up to the fence.

steps.title: What the neighbor may do with roots that spread into his field
steps.stepSummary: If the tree's roots spread into the neighbor's field, he may dig three טפחים deep so the roots do not block his plow. If he is digging a pit, ditch or cave, he may cut down through the roots as deep as he needs, and the wood belongs to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If roots were spreading into his neighbor's field, the neighbor may dig down three handbreadths so they do not get in the way of his plow. If he was digging a pit, a ditch or a cave, he cuts through and keeps going down, and the wood is his.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with the case of tree roots that grow under the neighbor's land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For ordinary plowing, the neighbor may cut roots only down to three טפחים, because that is the depth a plow reaches. When he digs a pit, ditch or cave, he may cut as deep as his digging needs. In that case he even keeps the root wood.

keyTerms.meaning: Pit, ditch and cave, three kinds of holes dug in the ground

phrases.english: If roots were spreading
into his fellow's field
he digs down three handbreadths
phrases.notes: "He" is the owner of the field the roots grew into. He may cut the roots as he digs.

phrases.english: so that they will not hold back the plow
If he was digging a pit, a ditch or a cave
he cuts and goes down
and the wood is his
phrases.notes: "His" means the man doing the digging, not the owner of the tree.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיוּ שׇׁרָשִׁים יוֹצְאִים לְתוֹךְ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same משנה with a related case about roots
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The neighbor may cut the roots down to plowing depth. When digging a pit, ditch or cave, he may cut as deep as he needs and keep the wood.

steps.title: The four cubits are for working the vineyard
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains that the four אמות of the משנה give the owner room to work his vineyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: A תנא taught: the four cubits that the Sages mentioned are there for the work of the vineyard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by quoting a teaching that gives the reason behind the four אמות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The distance gives the owner enough space to work his vines with his plow and animals. That way he does not have to go into his neighbor's field. This reason prepares the ground for שמואל's statement that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: A teacher of the ברייתא taught

phrases.english: GEMARA
A tanna taught
The four cubits that they said
are for the work of the vineyard

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא: אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שֶׁאָמְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason for the משנה's four אמות
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The four אמות leave room for working the vineyard.

steps.title: שמואל: in בבל two אמות are enough
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says the four-אמות rule applies only in ארץ ישראל. In בבל, two אמות are enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: They taught this only about ארץ ישראל. In בבל, two cubits are enough.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל limits the משנה's rule to ארץ ישראל and gives a smaller distance for בבל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The distance depends on how much room the work of the vineyard needs. שמואל holds that in בבל the work needs less room, so two אמות are enough there. The rule stays the same, but the measurement changes from place to place.

phrases.english: Shmuel said
They taught this only in the Land of Israel
but in Babylonia, two cubits

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the משנה's rule by location
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Four אמות in ארץ ישראל, two אמות in בבל.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports שמואל
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says two אמות, but the משנה says four. The only way both can be true is שמואל's split between ארץ ישראל and בבל, so the גמרא concludes that the ברייתא supports him.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is also taught in a ברייתא: A person may not plant a tree near his neighbor's field unless he keeps it two cubits away. But we learned in the משנה: four cubits! So isn't it clear that this follows שמואל? Yes, learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא as proof for שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא and the משנה give different numbers for the same rule. The way to make them agree is to say they speak about different places, exactly as שמואל said. That is why the ברייתא counts as support for שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: This is also taught in a ברייתא
But didn't we learn in the משנה
Learn from it, the proof stands

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's four אמות and the ברייתא's two אמות do not argue. One speaks about ארץ ישראל and the other about בבל.

phrases.english: It is also taught so
A person may not plant a tree
near his fellow's field
unless he distanced it from it
two cubits
But we learned: four cubits!
Rather, is it not as Shmuel said?
Learn from it

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא נָמֵי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source that supports שמואל's statement
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's rule that two אמות are enough in בבל
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that says two אמות, which can only fit with the משנה through שמואל's split between places

steps.title: Another version: the משנה and the ברייתא contradict each other
steps.stepSummary: In a second version, the same two sources are set against each other as a contradiction: the משנה says four אמות, while the ברייתא says two.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some present this as a contradiction. We learned in the משנה: A person may not plant a tree near his neighbor's field unless he keeps it four cubits away. But a ברייתא teaches: two cubits!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the discussion. Here the two sources clash, which sets up שמואל's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the ברייתא was a proof for שמואל. In this version, the same ברייתא is a problem that needs solving. Both versions end at the same law.

keyTerms.meaning: Some present it as a contradiction

phrases.english: And there are those who raise it as a contradiction
We learned: A person may not plant a tree
near his fellow's field
unless he distanced it from it
four cubits
But it is taught: two cubits!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְּרָמֵי לַהּ מִירְמֵא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the same material as a contradiction instead of a proof
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא gives the same rule with a different number, two אמות, so the two sources seem to clash.

steps.title: שמואל answers: one source is about בבל, the other about ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: שמואל resolves the contradiction. The ברייתא's two אמות is for בבל, and the משנה's four אמות is for ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: It is not difficult. Here it speaks about בבל, and there it speaks about ארץ ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers the contradiction by saying each source speaks about a different place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, שמואל's split between places is offered as the answer to a contradiction. In the first version, the same idea was his own statement, which the ברייתא then supported. Either way, the law is the same: four אמות in ארץ ישראל and two in בבל.

keyTerms.meaning: Here... there, each source speaks about a different case

steps.whatToRemember: Both versions arrive at the same law: four אמות in ארץ ישראל and two in בבל.

phrases.english: Shmuel said: It is not difficult
Here, in Babylonia
phrases.notes: "Here" points to the ברייתא's two cubits.

phrases.english: there, in the Land of Israel
phrases.notes: This "here" points to the משנה's four cubits.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in the previous step
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different places: each source applies to a different location
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה and the ברייתא argue about the same case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה speaks about ארץ ישראל and the ברייתא about בבל, so they do not argue.

steps.title: Birds from the palm trees damage רב יוסף's vineyard
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר רב חנן's palm trees stand on the border of רב יוסף's vineyard. Birds sit on the trees and then damage the vineyard, so רב יוסף tells him to cut the trees down.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא בר רב חנן had palm trees on the border of רב יוסף's vineyard. Birds would come, sit on the palm trees, then fly down into the vineyard and damage it. רב יוסף said to him: Go cut them down.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a story that shows the distance rules being used in real life. This step sets up the argument that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The trees themselves do not touch the vineyard. The damage comes from birds that use the trees as a resting place. רב יוסף still holds the tree owner responsible and asks him to remove the trees.

keyTerms.meaning: An orchard or planted field (here, a vineyard)

phrases.aramaic: רָבָא בַּר רַב חָנָן הֲווֹ לֵיהּ הָנְהוּ דִּיקְלֵי,
phrases.english: Rava bar Rav Chanan had certain palm trees
on the border of Rav Yosef's vineyard.
Birds would come and sit on the palm trees,
and come down into the vineyard and damage it.
He (Rav Yosef) said to him: Go cut them down.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא בַּר רַב חָנָן הֲווֹ לֵיהּ הָנְהוּ דִּיקְלֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a real-life case that applies the משנה's distance rule for trees.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב יוסף demands that the palm trees be cut down because they cause damage to his vineyard.

steps.title: The tree owner says he kept the required distance
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר רב חנן objects that he already kept his trees the required distance from the border.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: But I kept them the proper distance away!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר רב חנן pushes back on רב יוסף's demand. He says he followed the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה requires a tree to be planted a set distance from a neighbor's field. רבא בר רב חנן argues that since he kept that distance, he has done nothing wrong and should not have to cut anything.

phrases.english: He said to him: But I kept them distant!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אַרְחֵיקִי לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב יוסף's demand to cut the trees.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's demand to cut down the palm trees
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the legally required distance was kept, the tree owner should not be responsible for the damage.

steps.title: Vines need more distance than trees
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that the standard distance is only for trees. Vines need more.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: That rule is for trees, but for vines we need more distance.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף answers the objection. He says the usual distance is not enough when the neighbor's field has vines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף does not deny that the distance was kept. He says the rule of that distance only covers trees. Because his field has vines, a bigger distance applies, so the trees are still too close.

phrases.english: He said to him: That applies to trees,
but for vines we need more.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי מִילֵּי לְאִילָנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection that the required distance was kept.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of the distance rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The standard distance covers every kind of planted field.
steps.terutzMaskana: The standard distance is for trees. Vines need a greater distance.

steps.title: The משנה says vines and trees are the same
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר רב חנן quotes the משנה, which treats vines and all trees the same.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned in the משנה: both vines and any tree are the same!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר רב חנן challenges רב יוסף's answer from the words of the משנה itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says outright that the distance rule is the same for vines and for any tree. That seems to contradict רב יוסף's claim that vines need more.

keyTerms.meaning: Both this and that (are the same)

phrases.english: But we learned in the משנה:
both vines and any tree!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אֲנַן תְּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב יוסף's answer in step 17 using the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's claim that vines need more distance
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה explicitly puts vines and trees together under one distance rule.

steps.title: Same kind next to same kind is different from a tree next to vines
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף explains that the משנה is talking about a tree next to a tree, or vines next to vines. A tree next to vines needs more distance.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: That applies to a tree next to a tree and vines next to vines. But a tree next to vines needs more.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף explains how the משנה fits with what he said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף reads the משנה as covering two similar plants next to each other. A mixed case, with a tree on one side and vines on the other, is not covered by the משנה and needs a greater distance.

keyTerms.meaning: A tree next to another tree

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָנֵי מִילֵּי אִילָן לְאִילָן
phrases.english: He said to him: That applies to a tree next to a tree
and vines next to vines,
but a tree next to vines needs more.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי מִילֵּי אִילָן לְאִילָן וּגְפָנִים לִגְפָנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the משנה in step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the scope of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה gives one distance for vines and trees in every combination.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה covers only like next to like. A tree next to vines needs more distance.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the rule that a tree next to a neighbor's vines needs more than the standard distance.

steps.title: The tree owner refuses to cut the trees himself
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר רב חנן says he will not cut down the trees himself, because cutting a fruit-producing palm is forbidden and dangerous. He quotes רב and רבי חנינא. רב יוסף may cut them if he wishes.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I will not cut them down. רב said that a palm tree that produces a קב of fruit may not be cut down. And רבי חנינא said: My son שכחת died only because he cut down a fig tree before its time. If the Master wants, let him cut them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר רב חנן accepts that the trees may be cut. He brings two sources to explain why he personally will not do it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב teaches that cutting down a palm tree that still produces a קב of fruit is forbidden. רבי חנינא adds a story showing how dangerous it is to cut a fruit tree too early. So רבא בר רב חנן will not cut the trees himself, but he tells רב יוסף that he may cut them if he wants.

keyTerms.meaning: A קב, a measure of volume (here, of fruit)

steps.confusionAlert: רבא בר רב חנן is not saying the trees can stay. He agrees they may be cut down. He only refuses to be the one who cuts them.

phrases.english: He said to him: I will not cut them down,
for Rav said:
A palm tree that carries a kav of fruit,
it is forbidden to cut it down.
phrases.notes: This connects to the מצוה not to destroy fruit trees (דברים 20:19).

phrases.english: And Rabbi Chanina said:
My son Shichchat died
only because he cut down a fig tree before its time.
The Master, if it suits him, let him cut.
phrases.notes: "The Master" is a polite way of saying "you," meaning רב יוסף.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲנָא לָא קָיֵיצְנָא, דְּאָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After losing the argument, the tree owner explains why he still will not do the cutting himself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A palm tree producing a קב of fruit may not be cut down. So the owner will not cut it, but the damaged neighbor may.
steps.whatToRemember: A tree next to vines needs extra distance. Still, because cutting fruit trees is forbidden and dangerous, the tree owner left the cutting to the neighbor.

steps.title: רב פפא finds his neighbor cutting his trees' roots
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא's palm trees stand on the border of רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע's land. He finds רב הונא digging and cutting the roots, and asks what he is doing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא had palm trees on the border of רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע. He went and found him digging and cutting the roots. He said to him: What is this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a second story about trees on a border. It ends with רב פפא's question, which sets up רב הונא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the neighbor is not asking the owner to cut. He is cutting the roots himself. רב פפא wants to know what gives him the right to damage another person's trees.

phrases.aramaic: רַב פָּפָּא הֲווֹ לֵיהּ הָנְהוּ דִּיקְלֵי
phrases.english: Rav Pappa had certain palm trees

phrases.aramaic: אַמִּיצְרָא דְּרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ.
phrases.english: on the border of Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua.
He went and found him digging,
and cutting its roots.
He said to him: What is this?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי הַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story about trees on a border, this time about roots.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: By what right רב הונא is cutting the roots of רב פפא's trees.

steps.title: רב הונא quotes the משנה allowing him to dig three טפחים
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא answers from a משנה: if roots spread into a neighbor's field, the neighbor may dig three טפחים deep so the roots do not block his plow.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: We learned in a משנה: If roots were spreading into another person's field, he may dig down three טפחים so they do not hold back the plow.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא answers רב פפא's question by quoting a משנה that permits what he is doing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives a field owner the right to clear roots up to three טפחים deep, since that is the depth a plow works. Roots that reach this depth inside his own field may be cut.

keyTerms.meaning: Hold back, get in the way

phrases.english: He said to him: We learned in the משנה:

phrases.aramaic: הָיוּ שׇׁרָשִׁים יוֹצְאִים לְתוֹךְ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ –
phrases.english: If roots were going out into the field of another,
he digs down three,
phrases.notes: Three טפחים (handbreadths). The field owner may cut the roots down to that depth.

phrases.english: so that it not hold back the plow.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, תְּנַן: הָיוּ שׇׁרָשִׁים יוֹצְאִים לְתוֹךְ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב פפא's question from step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A משנה permits a field owner to dig three טפחים deep and cut a neighbor's roots so they do not block his plow.

steps.title: רב פפא objects that רב הונא is digging too deep
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא challenges רב הונא: the משנה he quoted only allows three טפחים, but רב הונא is digging deeper.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to him: That rule only allows three handbreadths, but you, sir, are digging deeper!
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא turns רב הונא's own proof against him. The משנה gives a limit of three טפחים, and רב הונא is going past it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 22, רב הונא used the משנה that lets a neighbor dig three טפחים so roots do not block his plow. רב פפא says that משנה sets a limit, not a free pass. Digging below three טפחים is more than the משנה allows.

keyTerms.meaning: This rule applies only to... (it limits a rule)
Master, a respectful way to say 'you'

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רב פפא speaking to רב הונא.

phrases.english: This rule applies only up to three [handbreadths],
but the Master is digging more!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי מִילֵּי שְׁלֹשָׁה, מָר קָא חָפַר טְפֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof רב הונא gave in Step 22 by pointing to that משנה's own limit.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's use of the three-טפחים משנה to justify his digging
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה allows only three טפחים, and רב הונא is digging deeper, so the source does not cover what he is doing.

steps.title: רב הונא answers that he is digging pits, which have no depth limit
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא says he is digging pits, ditches and caves. A different משנה lets such a digger cut roots all the way down and keep the wood.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I am digging pits, ditches and caves, as we learned in a משנה: If someone was digging a pit, a ditch or a cave, he may cut the roots as he goes down, and the wood is his.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא changes his reason. He is not digging for plowing. He is digging pits, so a different משנה applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The three-טפחים limit is for plowing, because a plow only goes that deep. Someone digging a בור, שיח or מערה needs to go deeper, and the משנה lets him keep cutting roots as he goes down. It even says the cut wood belongs to him.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה
He cuts and keeps going down

steps.confusionAlert: This does not cancel the three-טפחים rule. That rule is for plowing. Digging a pit is a different case with its own משנה.

phrases.english: He said to him:

phrases.aramaic: אֲנָא בּוֹרוֹת שִׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת קָא חָפַרְנָא –
phrases.english: I am digging cisterns, ditches, and caves –
as we learned in a משנה:
If he was digging a cistern, a ditch, or a cave –
he may cut and go down,
and the wood is his.
phrases.notes: The 'wood' is the pieces of root he cuts off.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲנָא בּוֹרוֹת שִׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת קָא חָפַרְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב פפא's challenge by saying the digging falls under a different משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: digging pits, not plowing, so a different source applies.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב הונא is relying on the plowing משנה, which allows only three טפחים.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is digging pits, ditches and caves, which may go down with no limit, and the cut wood is his.

steps.title: רב פפא admits his arguments did not convince רב הונא
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא reports that he gave רב הונא every argument he had, but could not win.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: I told him all of them, but I could not overcome him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא, telling the story later, says none of his proofs convinced רב הונא. This sets up the next move in the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא admits that none of his arguments, including the three-טפחים limit from step 23, convinced רב הונא. רב הונא's answer from step 24, the pit-digging משנה, held up. The line is not finished, and the story continues right after it.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
I told him all of them,
but I was not able to beat him;

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: אֲמַרִי לֵיהּ כּוּלְּהִי, וְלָא יְכֵילִי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sums up the back-and-forth and admits רב הונא's answers held, setting up what follows.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב פפא could not convince רב הונא with any of his arguments.
